summary: Welcome to the team. What your first week covers, day by day.
body:

Welcome to the team. Your first week is all about:

- Building confidence
- Celebrating small wins
- Coaching the basic systems and applying them
- Practising over and over again
- Creating independence

| Time | What |

| 09:30 | Planning meeting (09:00 on Monday and Saturday) |
| 10:00 | Sector leaders meeting |
| 10:30 | COD workshops: everyone, all stages |
| 11:00 | Primetime: individual sales coaching |

### Day 1: Induction Day

Your first impression of our business.

- Introduction to the business
- Expectations

**Primetime:** closing · taking control · rehash

- Morning wake-up call

- Break the day down
- Fill in the weekly tracker and analyse the numbers
- Plan for next week

### 2nd Week: Independent Growth

- Every day: recap all sales systems and practise the script
- Fill in any gaps in knowledge to help you become more independent
- Start COD stage 2: example setting and leadership knowledge
- Work through every impact with your coach so you have all the relevant information, skillset and knowledge

Every top performer started exactly where you are right now.

- We introduce customers to an old concept in a new way, giving them the opportunity to try new things

## Learning Styles Questionnaire

Pick the answer that feels **most like you**

**Question 1** — When spelling a word do you:

A. Forget names but remember faces

A. Flicking through a newspaper or magazine

A. Prefer verbal directions  
B. Prefer a written diagram/map  
C. Step into your car and find your own way

**Question 7** — When installing a new appliance do you:

A. Ignore the instructions and figure it out as you go  
B. Get someone to read the manual and tell you what to do  
C. Follow the guidelines in the instruction manuals

**Question 8** — During a lecture or meeting do you:

A. Prefer to discuss it with others to secure your understanding  
B. Like to actively participate whenever possible

A. Writer, journalist, lawyer  
B. Artist, architect, engineer, mechanic, interior designer

**Question 10** — Which of the following best suits you:

A. I participate in sport and generally excel  
B. I enjoy listening to music and often sing or hum to myself

**Your learning style: Visual** — You are a visual learner — you think in pictures and learn best by seeing. Make the most of the pitch card, diagrams and written materials when on the doors.

**Your learning style: Auditory** — You are an auditory learner — you learn best through listening and talking. Role-play conversations, listen to others rehash, and talk through the steps out loud.

**Your learning style: Kinesthetic** — You are a kinesthetic learner — you learn best by doing. Get on the doors as quickly as possible and learn through real-world experience.

### Know your learning style

**Visual** `Average population: 35%`  `Marketing companies: 59%`

- Learn through seeing
- Think in pictures
- Often sit at the front to avoid obstructions
- May take detailed notes
- Need to see presenter's body language and facial expressions to fully understand content

**Auditory** `Average population: 25%`  `Marketing companies: 5%`

- Learn through what they hear
- Written information may have little meaning until heard
- Like to talk things through, be involved in discussion and listen to others

**Kinesthetic** `Average population: 40%`  `Marketing companies: 40%`

- Learn through moving, doing and touching
- They like to try things out
- Find it hard to sit still and can be easily distracted
- Like to move around and gesture when talking and may be poor listeners

title: The Story
summary: The Modern Milkman in a nutshell.
body:
## The Modern Milkman in a nutshell

- Started as an idea that became a dream that turned into reality
- Launched in Colne, East Lancashire, by four friends delivering milk
- Started with only a few customers, now delivering to thousands of happy customers
- Inspired by Blue Planet and David Attenborough

### Blue Planet

The Blue Planet is a nature documentary series created and produced by the BBC and narrated by David Attenborough. The series examines marine life and how plastic and pollution affect its habitat.

The Blue Planet was an inspiration for four friends who were shocked by the heart-breaking scenes of plastic pollution in our ocean. After hearing famous words by Sir David Attenborough, they decided to join forces and combine a traditional milk round with modern technology, to go on a mission to bring it back and help reduce plastic.

> “Never before have we had such an awareness of what we are doing to the planet, and never before have we had the power to do something about that. The future of humanity and indeed, all life on earth, now depends on us.”

This is the quote from Sir David that inspired our four founders to create The Modern Milkman.

### Did you know?

88% of people who watched Blue Planet changed the way they think about using and disposing of plastic. The viewers were motivated to change their lifestyle after watching the pilot whale grieve over her dead calf killed by plastic; the albatross raising a plastic bag, mistaking it for her young; the turtle ensnared in a plastic bag; the whale trying to eat a plastic bucket (Global Citizen).

### Plastic saved

At the time the coaching booklet was written:

- **57,005,152** plastic bottles saved, and still counting
- **135,883** wheelie bins of plastic saved from landfill

> These numbers go up every day. Always refer to the latest update on The Modern Milkman website before you quote one.

title: How It Works
summary: The customer's milk round journey in three steps.
body:
## The customer's milk round journey

### 1 · Create a repeat weekly order

- Help the customer choose the products they need and use on a day-to-day basis.
- Modern Milkman is not only about milk. Customers can also create their order from an amazing range of fresh products: milk, eggs, juices, milkshakes, bread, cereals, treats and others.
- We also offer a household range, coffee, tea, fruit and veg boxes and many more.
- Customers can add extra products at any time before 8pm the night before their delivery.

### 2 · We deliver to your doorstep

- Regular weekly deliveries straight from the farms to your doorstep.
- Customers can spread their deliveries over 3 days: Mon, Wed, Fri or Tue, Thu, Sat, depending on the area they live in.
- There is a small delivery charge depending on the order value for the day.
- We deliver between 10pm and 7:30am so everyone has their fresh produce on their doorstep, ready to start the day right with a perfect breakfast!
- Customers don't need to be home for delivery.

### 3 · Rinse, return, reuse and repeat

- All our drinks come in returnable glass bottles, which we collect, wash and reuse.
- All you have to do is enjoy your products, rinse the bottles and put them out on your doorstep for us to collect and reuse.
- Even our tea and coffee come in returnable metal caddies.
- Any packaging that isn't reusable is plastic free, recyclable or home-compostable (including our teabags).

title: Need to Know
summary: Product information that every customer should know.
body:
When representing Modern Milkman and signing up new customers it is very important that we deliver a clear but thorough message. There is certain information that cannot be missed out from our conversations. It helps the customer understand the product and the service better, which leads to long-term retention.

1. **How much discount does the customer get?**  
   20% off their first 2 weeks, plus extra discounts for recommending friends and family.

2. **When does the customer pay for their first order?**  
   The customer pays for their first order then and there, at the point of the sale, to activate the discount and secure the spot on the milk round.

3. **How often does the customer pay?**  
   Weekly: 3 days before their first delivery day.

4. **What day does the payment get taken?**  
   First delivery day minus 3 days = that day.

5. **From when can a customer amend an order?**  
   Customers can start amending their orders at any time after they've received their first order. In the meantime, they can also add any extras or one-off products if they wish and will be charged accordingly.

6. **Can the customer add extra products to their order?**  
   Customers can add extra products at any time via our easy-to-use app. They can add products to their repeat order or as “one-offs”.

7. **What is the deadline for the customer to add extras to their order?**  
   The deadline to add any extra products is 8pm the night before the delivery.

8. **What days do we deliver?**  
   We deliver 3 times a week. Depending on the area our deliveries are scheduled for Mon, Wed, Fri or Tue, Thu, Sat.

9. **Can I pause my deliveries when I'm away?**  
   The customer has full control of their orders and deliveries by managing them through the app. They can pause their deliveries at any time in the future when they are away.

10. **Why do I need to set up weekly repeat orders? Can I just order once?**  
    The customer can order one-off products to be delivered on delivery days for which they already have a repeat order set up. This is because we need to collect and reuse their empty bottles.

11. **What do I do when I have not received my delivery or have missing items?**  
    Customers can contact customer services at any time or use the live chat, where online assistants are ready to help and answer their queries.

12. **Where does the produce come from?**  
    All our produce comes from independent UK farms and businesses. Except a few fruit and veg items it's all UK sourced.

13. **What happens if they add to or take away from the order?**  
    Taking away: they will pay less accordingly. Adding: the customer will pay accordingly. Weekly repeat orders will be added to their weekly billing; one-off products will be charged immediately.

14. **What details do we take from the customer?**  
    Order number, postcode, order value (excluding delivery fee).

> Please always check the website for updates.

body:
## The Round

The Round is The Modern Milkman's membership club. Joining covers the delivery fee on every order, so *the price you see is the price you pay*.

### What a member gets

- **Delivery fee covered** on every order. This is the big one for most people.
- **A welcome gift** for new members, and a seasonal gift for annual members.
- **Member's Week offers:** member-only deals, with up to 40% off.
- **A monthly prize draw:** every member is entered each month. Annual members get a double entry.
- **A birthday gift and a sign-up anniversary gift:** a coupon for one selected product.

### What it costs the customer

| Plan | Price | Works out at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monthly | £8.95 a month | about £2.06 a week |
| Annual | £89.95 a year | about £1.70 a week |

> Prices and benefits are from The Modern Milkman's website and can change. Check the website or the app before you quote one.

### The rules, in short

- The customer must be 18 or over.
- They can join during their first order, with you at the door.
- It is paid up front, monthly or yearly, and renews until they cancel.
- They can cancel at any time in the app. Their benefits carry on to the end of the period they have paid for.
- There is a 14-day cooling-off period.

### What it means for you

- The Round can be taken with a Silver sign-up or a Gold sign-up. A customer can also sign up without it.
- Each sign-up that takes The Round adds **£8** to your fee.
- It is paid a week after your sign-up fee, because of the 14-day cooling-off period.
- Our aim is **75% or more** of your sign-ups taking The Round.

Never tell a customer they have to take The Round to sign up, and never add it for them. Explain it clearly and let the customer choose.

title: Problems We Solve
summary: Problem = solution. Listen first, then fit The Modern Milkman to the customer's life.
body:
## Problem = Solution

### The problems our customers have

- Busy life, no time
- Ran out of milk again
- Empty fridge
- No ideas for breakfast, or last-minute ideas for breakfast in the morning
- Forgot to buy milk, again
- Plastic packaging everywhere
- Would love to help the environment but don't know how
- Farms are too far away, no fresh dairies in the area
- Overcrowded supermarkets, too many trips to the corner shop
- Online shopping with a minimum spend, slow deliveries
- Lack of taste, short shelf-life
- Lactose intolerant

> Did you know? The average person in the UK spends 47 minutes shopping each time they go to the supermarket! In a world that is increasingly time-poor, in which people work long hours, Modern Milkman is a great solution to this.

### Listen first

Once you understand the customer's needs, you are able to present them with different options. Indicate which solution you have for the customer's problem. Rather than presenting them with all the options available straight away, listen first and tailor the options to fit the needs of the customer.

**Example:** If a customer indicates that they only drink oat milk, talk about our fresh oat milk. It is not necessary to present all types of milk. If the customer says that they don't drink milk at all, show your interest by asking whether they are intolerant or just don't like it, and move straight away to other amazing products.

### Paint the picture

After explaining the different options to the customer, you can give them an idea of what their daily life will look like with Modern Milkman.

> “Imagine you are having a chilled Saturday morning after a long week at work, the kids are waiting in the kitchen for breakfast, and you realise there is no milk for their favourite cereals. You then have two options: get dressed and run to the corner shop to make the kids happy, or change their breakfast. With Modern Milkman, you can literally order by 8pm and your fridge will already be filled with fresh milk and products by 7:30am. One less worry after a busy week!”

This is the phase of the pitch where you create a desire with the customer. You can only create this desire if you carefully listen to the customer's home situation. This way you can respond to the needs and frustrations of the customer.

title: The Forbidden 'Local'
summary: Why we never use the word 'local' to sell The Modern Milkman, and what to say instead.
body:
## Why we shouldn't use the term 'local'

We should NOT be using the term local to sell our business.

- We are not a local business
- We do not use local suppliers, therefore our products are not local
- As we've grown as a business, some dairies are now far out, and independent suppliers are not local to most customer homes
- By using the term local, we are causing reputational and brand damage, as we are mis-selling to prospective customers

## What we can use instead of 'local'

Instead of using the term 'local', there are other ways to describe where the products are supplied from.

**Fruit & veg**

> Our fruit and veg is from suppliers that work hard to source fresh, quality produce with sustainable business practices and deliver in paper bags, so all you have to do is pop it into your recycling bin or compost heap when you're done.

**Milk**

> We work with and support a network of independent British dairies who help us to reduce plastic waste, as their products are delivered in return-and-reuse glass bottles.

**Bakery**

> All our baked goods are made by independent bakers and are delivered in sustainable packaging.

### General rule

> Use **independent suppliers**, NOT local.

title: Body Language & S.E.E.
summary: S.E.E.: three steps to a successful sales conversation.
body:
## S.E.E. Principle

Smile, eye contact and enthusiasm are among the most basic and universal indicators of openness, friendliness, relaxation and likeability. A smile is a powerful asset that helps establish rapport and build relationships. We are the ones that create a customer.

### S — Smile

- Contagious (people will laugh with you)
- Welcoming, friendly and polite
- Builds a relationship with the customer (likeability factor: make a “1-minute friend”)
- Relaxes the customer, makes them feel comfortable
- Makes you look attractive and approachable
- People like talking to happy people
- Makes customers think you are having a great time
- Shows amazing customer service

### E — Eye Contact

- Builds trust
- Shows confidence and honesty
- It is rude to talk to someone and not maintain eye contact
- Makes the customer feel special and important
- Engages the customer in the conversation
- Shows that you know what you are talking about

### E — Enthusiasm

- Creates curiosity, making your conversation attractive
- Makes you different from the last person they spoke to
- The customer will think that what you are saying is great
- Engages customers in the conversation
- Put on the show (it creates interest and is infectious)
- Your excitement and enthusiasm will rub off on customers
- Buys you time and helps you relate and impulse them

> It's not what you are saying, it is how you are saying it: tone of voice.

## Body Language

The most important component of face-to-face communication.

- **55%** Body language
- **38%** Tone of voice
- **7%** Words

Customers will read our body language, so we need to be conscious to display the right message. Customers may see you before you knock on their door.

### Body Language

- L shape, sideways
- One arm's length away from the door
- Opposite the door handle
- S.E.E. before you knock
- Respect personal space
- Lean back, relaxed
- Controlled hand gestures
- Confident and friendly approach
- Nod to show acknowledgment
- Always agree with the customer to show active listening
- Walk with purpose. Head up, chest out
- Knock with confidence
- Point with a straight arm when you close
- Give the pitch card with a straight arm

### Tone of Voice

- Take a deep breath before you knock so you can control the speed of your voice
- Clear, concise and confident
- Enthusiastic, genuine
- Use buzz words to keep engagement, e.g. Amazing, Brilliant, Great, Really?
- Emphasise key words
- Fluctuate your voice to attract the customer

Everyone has heard “it's not what you said, it's the way you said it” before. This is so true. You can say the right thing, but in the wrong way, which affects the outcome. There are 2 aspects to using your tone of voice:

- **Volume** shows confidence. You always need to be 1 volume louder than the customer, so you are in control.
- **Frequency:** when saying “good points”, you need a higher frequency, so people know it's good.

### Words

- Clear message and communication
- Transparent and honest
- Short and simple, but interesting and impulsive

### 7 Observables

1. Facial expressions
2. Eyes
3. Gestures
4. Postures
5. Stance
6. Movements
7. Image

title: The 5 Steps
summary: The fundamentals of sales conversations.
body:
## What is the 5 Steps?

A very simple system to follow, to start and engage the potential customer in a conversation about the product or service we are representing. This system is used across all brands, and its transparency allows us to learn how to represent any brand in the future.

### 1 · Introduction — Goal: to grab attention

- First impression is the last impression
- Customers judge us within the first 7–15 seconds
- RELATE to them (kids, dogs, garden, holidays, cars, football, sport, current issues)
- Use ICE BREAKERS (“Don't worry, it's nothing serious, just from the milkman”)
- Qualify the customers early: speak to the decision maker
- Set up call backs if needed

### 2 · Presentation — Goal: to create interest

- Paint the picture
- Concept: how it works
- Use the Pitch Card and the Power of the Pen
- G.I.F.T.S: impulse people to buy
- Give reasons to buy (features vs benefits)
- USPs: why people love it

### 3 · Short Story — Goal: to create a problem and solution

- Ask questions and use hooklines (get the agreement)
- Recommend the right products and options
- Build value in the Modern Milkman service and products
- Always have the customer in mind, and their benefits too
- Keep It Short and Simple
- Know your product
- Show passion and enthusiasm

### 4 · Close — Goal: to close the deal

- Get agreement
- Explain how to get involved
- Take control (Point, Explain, Tell)
- Assume the sale and expect YES: it's a great product
- Be confident and to the point
- Use pre-closes and hooklines

### 5 · Rehash — Goal: to create a long-term customer

- Consolidation of the sale
- Next steps and follow up
- Customer understanding and confidence
- Long-term feeling and impulse
- Leave behinds
key_facts: 1 Introduction · 2 Presentation · 3 Short Story · 4 Close · 5 Rehash
Introduction: to grab attention. Customers judge us within the first 7–15 seconds
Presentation: to create interest. Short Story: to create a problem and solution
Close: to close the deal. Rehash: to create a long-term customer

title: The Pitch
summary: The general Modern Milkman pitch, word for word.
body:
## The general Modern Milkman pitch

### Introduction

> Hi, you ok? Great.  
> Don't worry, it's nothing serious.  
> My name is ⟦text "your name"⟧ from The Modern Milkman.

> We deliver fresh milk and produce to neighbours in your area.  
> You've probably seen our vans around? *(nod)*

> **YES:** Great, you must be up early!  
> **NO:** That's ok, we deliver quite early!

*(Relate to the customer and listen to their hot spots.)*

### Presentation

> We became very popular and today we're just giving discounts to everyone.  
> I'm guessing you drink milk, yeah?  
> Perfect!  
> How many pints would you say you go through in the week?  
> Perfect!  
> I think you're going to love this!

*(Pass the pitch card.)*

### Short story

*(Front of the pitch card.)*

> What your neighbours love about us:

> **1.** Everything comes fresh from British farms, so you'll get the best quality.

> **2.** Milk comes in a glass bottle, do you remember those? And everything we do is plastic free, so it's good for the environment.

> **3.** And for your convenience and flexibility it's all done on our app, so you can order by 8PM in the evening and get it delivered by 7:30am in the morning!

> The only thing that we'd like you to do is rinse the bottles after you use them, leave them out on the doorstep, and we'll collect and reuse them. Is that ok?

*(Back of the pitch card.)*

> From these products here, which ones do you use regularly?

### Close

> My job today is really simple.  
> As I mentioned before, we're doing a discount for new customers and giving away 20% off their first 2 weeks, so everyone can experience our fresh produce and see how it fits into their lifestyle.

> Do you use iPhone or Android?  
> Perfect!  
> If you go grab your phone, I'll show you how it works. It only takes a few minutes; I'll just wait here.

> TIP: If the customer is on the fence, use a hookline, i.e. “Bit of a silly question...”

### Pre-close hookline

> “Bit of a silly question, but if you could get fresh milk (produce) straight from the farm delivered to your doorstep, I assume, like most of the neighbours I've spoken to today, you would jump on our milk round as well, yeah!”

## Adaptive selling

Adaptive selling is a tailored approach towards each individual customer, which takes into account the type of person in front of you, the sales situation and the feedback and answers received during the conversation. It's about figuring out what the other person wants and adapting your pitch to their preferences, so they get what they need out of the conversation.

1. **Match the customer's communication style.** Speak in a language and tone customers are familiar with.
2. **Understand the customer's social style.** This is also important for building rapport.
3. **Adapt to the sales situation.** Their needs and wants.

### Examples

- **I'm guessing you drink milk?** YES: carry on. NO: ask questions.
- **Are you in charge of the grocery shopping in the house?** YES: carry on. NO: ask questions: “I'm guessing it's the other half? Are they around?” If not, set up a call back.
- **Have you seen our vans?** NO: “That's fine, we deliver quite early.” YES: “Great, you must be an early bird.”
- **How much milk do you go through in the week?** A lot: ask questions: “How many pints? What milk do you usually get?” and carry on. Not much: ask questions to qualify: “How many pints would you say you go through in a week? No worries, I guess you eat eggs?” Keep asking questions about other products to see whether the customer is using what we offer. If not, apologise and politely leave.

There are many scenarios we could mention. Most important is the way we approach each situation: always ask questions, relate to their answers and be nice, polite and professional.

Short story: fresh from British farms · glass bottles, plastic free · order by 8pm, delivered by 7:30am
The ask: rinse the bottles, leave them on the doorstep, and we'll collect and reuse them
Close: 20% off the first 2 weeks. "Do you use iPhone or Android?"

title: The Pitch Card
summary: The power of the Pitch Card and the power of the Pen.
body:
## What?

- The pitch card is a great tool to explain the deal and current promotions in a short and simple way.
- When you're brand new it helps you remember what to say in your 5 steps conversation.
- It engages the customer and lets you know if the customer is paying attention.
- Easy for the customer to understand.
- People are naturally visual and it is easier for them to imagine the situation.
- The pitch card is designed to create engagement and to provide a visual tool for you and the customer.

## How?

- The key is getting the pitch card into the customer's hand. It's 9/10 of the sale.
- Guide it into the customer's hand, encourage them to take it and to look at the pitch card.
- If a customer does NOT take the pitch card, they are probably not interested.
- Keep a hold of the top, to stop them turning it over, until you are ready.
- Guide them where to look by pointing with your pen: the “POWER OF THE PEN”.
- Use it with your presentation, after the introduction, to show customers what you are talking about and what you are looking for.
- Take the pitch card out of the customer's hand and then ask questions.
- Use the pitch card or other collateral to turn objections, talking about the solutions we are providing so they'd want to get involved.
- Remember: if the customer looks at and takes the pitch card, it shows interest. If not, move on to the next one.
- After impulsing them, take the pitch card away and close.

## When?

- On the door, after qualifying, during the introduction
- Whenever you forget what to say next
- When talking about The Modern Milkman's products
- When the customer looks confused and has a service or product related question
- When the customer gives an objection

## The 'Power of the Pen'

People are visual creatures. Use your pen to point and create focus on the area you are talking about, and watch people's eyes follow your pen. It's like watching a tennis match. The pen allows your customers to see what you want them to pay attention to without your hand being in the way.

## What's on the card

### Front page impulses

- Reusable glass bottles
- Convenience with a conscience
- Flexible online ordering
- Fresh drinks and groceries
- No plastic waste
- The plastic waste saved so far, and the target

> Pitch cards get updated. Go by the card in your hand.

title: Ice Breakers & Relating
summary: How to start the conversation, and three steps to a successful introduction.
body:
## What is an ice breaker?

An ice breaker is a funny anecdote, an open question or a compliment that warms up the conversation between people. Ice breakers are helpful especially when starting a conversation with someone you don't know. An ice breaker can get people talking, generate laughter, and help people start with an initial level of comfort.

By breaking the ice, you are able to start a conversation with the potential customer and put them at ease. To break the ice, you can use what you see around you or a funny anecdote. Be yourself and have fun with it.

### Examples of ice breakers

- “How are you? Are you ok? How was your day?”
- “My name is ......”
- “I'm sure you've seen our vans before. Have you had a milkman before?”
- “Any plans for today? Any plans for the weekend? Any plans for Halloween / Xmas / half term / Valentine's?”
- “Who won an award for the best grocery shopping in the house?”
- “Whatever you are cooking smells incredible. Let me guess, is it chicken casserole?”
- “We couldn't catch you a few weeks back, I guess you were on holiday. How was it?”
- “We couldn't catch you earlier. I guess you had a busy day at work. I will keep it short, I promise.”

## 3 senses

9 out of 10 sales are done because the customer likes you, so it is vital to learn how to sell yourself and build relationships. Relating is aided by using observables. These are the things that you see, hear or smell when at a customer's house. Observables also help you to paint a picture of who you are talking to, so you can adjust the product appropriately.

| Sense | What to notice |
| --- | --- |
| **Hear** | Music, TV · Children, a party · Cars, people, dogs |
| **Smell** | Food, cooking, baking · Flowers, garden plants · Freshener |
| **See** | Pictures, furniture, ornaments · Decorations, toys · Dogs, kids, clothes |

> TIP: Avoid controversial conversations related to politics, sex, religion, sad and offensive topics. Watch your jokes and language so as not to upset anyone. Have fun but remain professional about it.

## Relating

### R — Recognise hot spots

- Listen carefully to spot the things that customers are into, so you can bring them up in your conversation
- Talk about what they love, what excites them
- Talk about them: people love talking about themselves

### E — Enjoy the conversation

- Be genuine, honest and friendly
- Don't be afraid to be yourself
- Don't be like a robot, don't be fake
- Have fun in your conversations

### L — Listen

- Show active listening skills by nodding and maintaining eye contact
- We all have two ears and one mouth: use them in the correct ratio
- Listen more, talk less
- Pay attention, focus on your customer

### A — Ask questions

- Any type of question to start the conversation
- Questions keep the customer engaged in the conversation
- Shows that you are interested in them and that you care

### T — Tailor your pitch

- Qualify and identify what type of customer you have in front of you, so you can adapt your intro and the conversation
- People buy for different reasons: be aware of their needs and wants and provide solutions specific to them

### E — Enthusiasm

- Creates curiosity, making your conversation attractive
- Makes you different from the last person they spoke to
- Customers will think that what you are saying is great
key_facts: 9 out of 10 sales are done because the customer likes you
Use what you HEAR, SMELL and SEE at the door to relate
R.E.L.A.T.E = Recognise hot spots, Enjoy the conversation, Listen, Ask questions, Tailor your pitch, Enthusiasm
Avoid controversial conversations: politics, sex, religion, sad and offensive topics

title: Law of Averages
summary: How work ethic always beats talent.
body:
## The principle of the L.O.A.

The more people we speak to, the more sales we will do. This means that the person who speaks to the most people will always do more sales. It's like scoring in football: if we take more shots, we will score more goals and beat the person with more skills. The L.O.A. is a system that guarantees everyday success.

The L.O.A. says that if you do something often enough a ratio will begin to appear. If you talk to 10 people, for example, and 1 says yes, a ratio will begin to appear: you are at 1:10. You'll notice that once it starts, it tends to continue. Talk to 10 more, get 1, and so on. In marketing and sales this is often referred to as a conversion rate.

### The numbers for a day

- **120** doors
- **80** people spoken to
- **20** qualified customers
- **15–20** phones / closes
- **6–10+** sign-ups

> On average, 40 people won't be home that day for various reasons, and 50–60 people won't qualify for different reasons. It's important we qualify each customer early and focus on following the L.O.A., not on results.

### Benefits of speaking to a lot of people

- More chances to find positive customers
- More situations and scenarios to learn from, quicker
- Getting more NOs builds your skillset and resilience
- A way of working the territory efficiently and effectively
- Work ethic always beats the skillset
- A great opportunity to develop the high level of work ethic and consistency needed to progress
- Focusing on the process, not results, helps in maintaining logical thinking and a positive approach to your day
- A great way to learn how to become solution orientated
- Builds our competitive edge and teaches us how to be data driven

> TIP: Objections are part of the process. Do not take “NO” personally. Qualify early. Only look for positive people. Focus on systems and work ethic.

## Who qualifies

| Qualifiers (able to sign up) | Non-qualifiers (unable to sign up) |
| --- | --- |
| Over 18. There is no upper age limit, as long as they are comfortable using the app | Under 18 |
| Tech-savvy: a smartphone and an active email | Not able to use the app or email |
| Decision makers: the person who does the shopping | Not the decision maker |
| Speaks English | Does not speak enough English to understand what they are signing up to |
| An “A” customer: positive, has time to talk, uses the products | Vulnerable, or not able to make their own decision |
|  | Already a customer, or has a local milkman |

**Interested:** potential buyers that will listen to you and want to talk to you. They are easy to impulse, answer and ask questions, have open body language, are generally positive about you, and have often heard about it.

**Not interested:** people who will not listen to you. The aim is to spend as little time as possible with them, to maintain our enthusiasm.

**Time wasters:** they listen to you, maybe even let you close them. A “yes, yes” person, generally taking control of the conversation. Impulse, close, leave.

## Believing in the Law of Averages

It gives us a chance to get the result we want and not get frustrated. Following the L.O.A. allows us to develop logical, numbers-based, data-driven thinking and prevents us from being emotional about our day.

There is no secret to high-volume sales: the more people we speak to each day, the more sales we will do and the more our skillset will grow.

- Let our attitude determine our sales, not sales determine our attitude.
- Do not take rejection personally.
- Have a sense of urgency: save time to speak to more people.
- Qualify people early in each conversation, and be careful not to pre-judge.
- The more people we speak to, the more sales targets we will hit. Every “NO” will ultimately bring us closer to a “YES”.
- Knock on the last door with the same enthusiasm as the first.
- Only look for positive people (or people you can make positive).
- Apply all the correct systems, not only the L.O.A. The sale is a combination of all systems working together.
- Visit at least 120 houses per day. If the territory is bigger than this, stop at 120 houses, as we will not have time to get around them all. The remaining territory can be left for the following day.
- Aim to go around the territory a minimum of 3 times, and if possible more. 1st lap: qualify & sell. 2nd lap: sell. 3rd lap: sell & call backs.
- Be prepared, so that you avoid delays getting into the field.
- Understand the L.O.A. in different territories and what work ethic is required to achieve the desired results.
- Understand the 3 types of days to train our mentality right: on any given day you cannot tell at what time your sales will come.
- Never give up: break the day down every 1–2 hours to see how far away we are from hitting the L.O.A. and to maintain logical thinking.
- Never give up: there is always a Mr and Mrs Smith in every territory, someone that likes us, likes the product and just loves buying new things.
- Enthusiasm powered by data: numbers don't lie, data shows the truth. Break the day down to see the patterns and where we need to improve the next day.

> Remember there is no magical pitch, there is no magical day, there is no magical system. IT'S ALL DOWN TO OUR WORK ETHIC, BASIC SYSTEMS AND MENTALITY.

### For every 100 people we see there will always be

- **YES** · Definite sales: interested, a straight yes
- **MAYBE** · Probable sales: customers on the fence
- **ONLY IF** · Possible sales: customers with objections
- **NO** · Definitely not sales: non-qualifiers or straight NOs

### Examples of the L.O.A. in real life

- A deck of cards: the ACES (if each ace is worth £20, what do you need to do to get it?)
- A bubble gum machine
- Football: strikers (how many shots do they need to score a goal?)
- Buying clothes, shoes or a new outfit
- Finding the perfect venue for a party
- Looking for a great birthday present
- Choosing the next holiday or city break
- Finding the right gym, club or activity
key_facts: The more people we speak to, the more sales we will do
A day: 120 doors · 80 people spoken to · 20 qualified customers · 15–20 phones / closes · 6–10+ sign-ups
On average 40 people won't be home that day and 50–60 won't qualify
Qualifiers: over 18 (no upper age limit), tech-savvy, decision makers, an active email, speak English
Go around the territory a minimum of 3 times: qualify & sell, sell, sell & call backs
"Let our attitude determine our sales, not sales determine our attitude."

title: G.I.F.T.S
summary: The five impulse factors: the different reasons why people buy.
body:
## Impulse factors

Becoming good at sales is simply a matter of becoming good at understanding people and raising their interest on a psychological level. Why do more people say no than yes? Because approximately 90% of the time, talk of savings is not enough to grab their interest.

The better you become at motivating people towards a product or service, the better your sales will be. Different impulses will motivate different people, so use all of these factors with every customer to cover all bases. Here are the five main impulse factors, also known as G.I.F.T.S. Use them throughout the first four steps.

### G — Greed

- Fresh milk, quality produce
- Supporting independent businesses
- The promotion, discounts
- Save time, convenient
- No waste, glass bottles
- No plastic, helping the environment
- Nostalgia, a great concept
- Easy to use app, you are in control
- Less stress, no worries
- Less shopping to do

### I — Indifference

- The opposite of desperate: relaxed body language and tone of voice
- “It's up to you”
- “My job”: removes you from the sale
- Make people feel comfortable
- Shrug your arms and nod your head

### F — Fear of loss

- Last few spaces in the van
- Missed you out in the week: “Sorry we couldn't catch you earlier, you must've been busy working?”
- Last day in the area
- “If I have time” (when setting up a call back)

### T — The Jones theory

- Seen the milk bottles on the doors, seen the vans
- Place name, street name
- Promote how popular we've become
- Say “just like everybody else” lots

> You can see why everyone is jumping on our milk round · Everyone else has got involved today · Most people in your area love supporting farms and independent suppliers · Most neighbours said the same thing · That was most popular today · Everyone is so nice in this area · You are so lucky to live in this area, great people around here

### S — Sense of urgency

- Hustle, don't stroll
- Have energy when talking
- Act like you are running out of spaces on the van
- Say “today” lots
key_facts: G.I.F.T.S = Greed, Indifference, Fear of loss, The Jones theory, Sense of urgency
Different impulses motivate different people, so use all of them with every customer
Indifference is the opposite of desperate: "It's up to you", "My job"
The Jones theory: "just like everybody else"

title: Hooklines
summary: Smart questions that get a small commitment before the big one.
body:
## What?

Hooklines are smart questions designed to get a small commitment from a customer. A small commitment will lead to a big commitment. It is an opportunity to check and verify whether the customer is ready to be closed, because they have been impulsed and are excited. These statements or questions allow customers to reflect on their daily routines, remind them about their problems and talk about their life. Using hooklines makes the customer open up and reassure themselves that they really need the product.

## When?

- When you see a buying sign
- Just before you close
- After a block or objection
- When you need to get commitment from the customer
- Throughout the whole 5 steps, to make the conversation flow

> TIP: Always use a hookline before you close a customer, to get the agreement.

## How?

- Be yourself
- Have fun creating new hooklines related to life situations and products
- Use statements and questions to engage the customer
- Show indifference
- Direct the conversation to where you want it to go
- Be enthusiastic about the topic of conversation
- Show understanding and acknowledge what the customer is saying
- Focus on the customer's hot spots: reducing plastic, easy to use, removing stress from your day, less to worry about, never run out of milk, supporting farms

### Starting phrases

- “I assume, like me...”, “I presume...”
- “I'm guessing, like most people...”
- “Like everyone that qualified today...”
- “Correct me if I'm wrong...”
- “Did I hear you right, you were saying...”
- “Bit of a silly question...”, “Bit of a daft one, please don't laugh...”
- “Imagine, if you could...”, “Imagine, a few months down the line...”
- “If we think about it, our life would be so much easier if...”

### Simple impulses to use with them

- “...if you were in total control, so you never had too much or too little, you'd be happy, yeah?”
- “...if you never had to run to the corner shop because you'd run out of the essentials, you'd be happy, yeah?”
- “...if you could support independent businesses and help the environment by getting your milk delivered in glass bottles to your door, you would, yeah?”

## The best hooklines

### Milk

- “I assume that if we drop fresh milk, straight from the dairy, in glass bottles, and you'd manage it with an app, you'd use it as well, yeah?”
- “I assume getting your milk delivered would make life a bit easier for you, wouldn't it, yeah?”
- “Have you ever gone to the fridge in the morning and there's no milk? Starts your day off on the wrong note, doesn't it?”
- “I assume you drink milk, yeah?”
- “How many pints do you normally have in a week?”
- “You know that feeling when the kids use most of the milk and just leave a bit without telling you?”
- “Do you know that pain when you fancy a quick glass of milk and you've run out?”
- “Do you remember those rainy mornings when you were running to the corner shop in your PJs just to get some milk for breakfast or coffee?”
- “Do you run out of milk often, or are you pretty planned?”

### Other products

- “I assume you have orange or apple juice at breakfast?”
- “Do you usually have cereal or toast in the morning? Ever have cereal in the evening?”
- “Do you normally make sandwiches for lunch, or are you more of a salad person?”
- “How are the kids with their fruit and vegetables?”
- “Are the kids more into milkshakes or fizzy pop?”
- “Who doesn't like to start their Sunday with a coffee or tea and a freshly baked pastry?”
- “What's everyone's favourite juice in the morning?”
- “Do you tend to make a flask of coffee for work in the morning?”
- “Lots of people love getting our eggs, for a quick omelette after a busy day.”
- “How do you like your eggs in the morning?”
- “Did it ever happen to you: you've done your shopping, come home, and you're unpacking your bags to realise that you forgot milk, bread, eggs or butter?”
- “Are you more of a tea or coffee person?”

### The milkman

- “Did you have a milkie growing up too? We just seemed to disappear, didn't we?”
- “Have you ever seen Bob, our milkman, in the morning?”
- “Did you have a milkman before? We've used technology to make ordering your milk easier. All you need to do is place the order and Modern Milkman will be right there for you.”
- “Everyone loves the modern way of milk deliveries and the simplicity of it.”
- “We all remember and love our traditional milkman.”

### Kids

- “I guess the kids have done projects at school about reducing plastic and helping the environment?”
- “Do you have the grandkids over quite often? What's their favourite breakfast?”
- “People love us, as it's hard to just pop to the shops when you are working and looking after the children.”
- “It's hard to just ‘pop’ to the shop when you have kids, isn't it?”

### Supporting farms

- “We use and support traditional, independent businesses and dairies. Bit of a silly question, but if you could get fresh milk delivered to your doorstep, knowing it comes fresh from the farm, I'm sure you would be happy, yeah?”
- “Nowadays our farms and independent businesses need us more than ever. That's why loads of people support smaller and family-run businesses.”

### The environment

- “Those big plastic milk bottles can be really heavy, can't they?”
- “I'm sure, like most people today, knowing the independent dairy gets a better deal by using us rather than the supermarkets, you'd be happy for us to deliver to you too, yeah?”
- “It can be hard trying to reduce plastic use, can't it?”
- “One of our main objectives as a company is to help reduce plastic consumption, to help protect the environment for future generations. I'm sure you'd be happy to be a part of that, yeah?”

### General

- “You should also keep an eye out for special treats just in time for Christmas, like our famous cheeses and sweet picks.”
- “Don't forget to tell your friends about us for further discounts on your deliveries!”
- “Check our website for the latest updates and some great eco warriors' articles.”

title: Asking Questions & Taking Control
summary: Whoever asks the question is in control of the conversation.
body:
## Why ask questions?

The questions you ask help you to uncover customers' needs and desires. They allow you to connect with them and demonstrate your expertise. By asking questions you can discover the real desires of your potential customer. It also allows you to qualify the sale and ensures that you and the customer are on the same page at any given time.

Sometimes all you need to do is ask one question, and the customer will share all the information you need. More often than not, you'll need to lead several lines of enquiry to get the full picture. Don't limit yourself to one type of question.

> REMEMBER: Whoever asks the question is in control of the conversation!

## Taking control

Taking control of a sales conversation isn't about being bossy, demanding or rude. It's about using relationship-building techniques, body language, tone of voice and questioning systems to help the customer make a decision. By doing this you find that taking control becomes natural and effortless, as opposed to forced and awkward. It is crucial to take control of the conversation from the beginning to the end. Always be light-hearted and subtle with it.

1. **Work toward a mutually beneficial outcome.**  
   To do this, you have to find out what the customer really wants. Ask questions to find out more about your customer's wants and needs.
2. **Get agreement from the customer on the steps needed to take the sale forward.**  
   If the customer is bought into the process by agreeing to it, then life becomes much easier.
3. **Remember to sell yourself rather than just your product or service.**  
   Sales is primarily an exchange between people: a transfer of your energy, enthusiasm and confidence. Listen to understand them, not just to respond. Speak with passion and conviction. Respect the customer.

| Verbal | Non-verbal |
| --- | --- |
| Asking questions | Eye contact |
| Finishing a sentence with YEAH | Stance: L shape, not square on |
| Asking “YES questions” (questions which lead the conversation where you want it to go) | Gestures, posture |
| Asking questions that you know the answers to | Facial expressions |
| Speaking with confidence and clarity | Movements matching your words |
| Relating, to help the customer feel comfortable | Professional dress code |
| Using hooklines and CLOSING after | Lively tone of voice, a smile |
| Turning objections and CLOSING after | Indifferent body language |
| Jokes, making a joke out of yourself | Give the customer space, ask the question, then wait for the answer |
| Stroking their ego | Use the pitch card |

## Different types of questions

1. **Fact-gathering questions**  
   Give you more insight and background on your customers. “Have you heard of us? Have you used us before? How long ago?” · “How much milk would you say you go through in a week?”

2. **Goal-assessment questions**  
   Once you know your customer's goals, you can demonstrate how your product will help achieve them. “Is having more time important to you? We are all so busy these days.” · “Would it make you happy if someone removed the stress of your weekly shopping?” · “Would it put a smile on your face if you knew your milkman will always be there?”

3. **Priority questions**  
   Identify the customer's most important objectives or challenges. “What annoys you the most about your breakfasts at the moment?” · “What is the biggest challenge that stops you from getting more fresh produce?”

4. **Thought-provoking questions**  
   Make the customer see things from a different perspective. “Did you know...?”, “Have you heard...?”, “Are you aware...?”, “Have you thought of...?”

5. **Hypothetical questions**  
   Require the customer to think about the future. “Imagine a few months down the line...” · “Fast-forward a few weeks from now...” Positive hypotheticals lead the customer to imagine a better future, preferably one with your product.

6. **Clarifying questions**  
   Let you check the customer understands, and make sure you're coming to the right conclusions. “Correct me if I'm wrong...?”, “Did I hear you right...?”, “What did you mean by saying...?”, “Is there anything I have not explained properly...?”

7. **Objection-surfacing questions**  
   If we don't get their objections out in the open, we can't address them. “Does anything about the product concern you?”, “What are your main concerns?” · “Are you happy to jump on board?”, followed by “Any reason why?” if they say no.

8. **Open questions**  
   Allow the customer to express themselves, as they require more than one-word answers. “Any dietary restrictions or intolerances?” · “What are you usually preparing for breakfast?” · “What is your favourite breakfast?”

9. **Assumptive questions**  
   Questions that we should know the answer to. They help connect with the customer and get them into the habit of saying yes. “I guess you've had days that you forgot to buy milk and eggs, yeah?” · “You would probably prefer milk fresh from the dairy, if it wasn't that far away, yeah?”
key_facts: Questions uncover the customer's needs, qualify the sale and keep you both on the same page
Taking control isn't about being bossy: it's relationship building, body language, tone of voice and questions
Nine types of question: fact-gathering, goal-assessment, priority, thought-provoking, hypothetical, clarifying, objection-surfacing, open, assumptive
Finish sentences with 'yeah' and ask 'yes questions'

title: The Objection Cycle
summary: How to effectively address customers' concerns.
body:
## The objection cycle

Often customers do not say YES straight away, and some of the sales you will make will come from handling the customer's objections. Objections do not necessarily mean that the customer is not interested, but can often mean that they are looking for more information. In fact objections are often signs of interest.

No matter what your experience level is at sales, you will always face objections from the customer. It's very easy to become frustrated, but if you understand that this is a natural part of sales you will soon learn to overcome them. Objections provide you with a great way to build credibility and move forward in the sale; they show that your customer is listening and considering buying from you.

1. **Smile & agree**  
   Use a buzzword and look happy about the fact a customer has just given you an objection! “Great!” · “Perfect” · “I know what you mean” · “I fully get that” · “Absolutely!” This will throw customers off, as they would expect you to panic. It creates further interest in what you've got to say next.

2. **Relate to others**  
   “A lot of people today have asked me the same.” · “Most of your neighbours said the same thing.” This lets the customer know that you're experienced in dealing with their concern, and that having a concern is a natural part of the conversation.

3. **Feel · Felt · Found**  
   “I know how you feel...” · “Most people felt the same way...” · “Until they found out...”

4. **Re-impulse**  
   Remind the customer of the BENEFITS of the product or service. Use impulses relevant to the customer in front of you. It is NOT one size fits all.

5. **Close**  
   Once we get an agreement from the customer and clear out all their concerns, we are ready to CLOSE the deal. If you have closed them previously, don't be afraid to repeat your close to reinforce the next steps.

## Two ways of handling objections

### 1 · Pre-empting

Dealing with the negative before it arises. Ideally objections are pre-empted, to prevent them from happening in the first place.

- “Sorry I couldn't catch you yesterday / earlier. I'm guessing you've been busy at work?”
- “I know you are busy, but I won't keep you long, I promise. We're just asking a few questions about...”
- “I know you've probably seen us deliver. My name is ... from ..., just looking for a quick chat with the person who does the shopping in the house. Is that yourself or someone else?”

### 2 · Turning

Dealing with the objection after it has arisen. To turn objections into opportunities you should:

- Acknowledge or show empathy for the customer's concerns
- Reframe the situation by verbalising your understanding
- Don't undo your efforts by using the word “BUT”!
- With your response, be concise and specific, and customise it to meet their needs

> If YES: “Great, that's exactly why I am here.”  
> If NO: “Great, that's exactly why I am here.”

## Types of objections

- **Product objection:** “I don't need it”
- **Source objection:** “I don't trust you”
- **Value objection:** price or money: “I can find it cheaper”, “It is too expensive”, “Out of my budget”
- **Need objection:** “I'm already satisfied”
- **Decision objection:** “I have to think about it”

| DO | DON'T |
| --- | --- |
| Stay calm | Panic |
| Smile, nod and agree | Pause or freeze |
| Be yourself | Become desperate or pushy |
| Have fun with it | Take yourself too seriously |
| Understand the customer's point of view | Take it personally |
| Suggest solutions | Be rude or patronising |
| Ask questions | Be robotic |
| Be polite and professional | Avoid the topic |
| Give a clear, short and sweet answer | Overcomplicate it for them |

## Buying signs and leaving signs

As well as verbal objections, body language and the flow of conversation can also help assess whether someone is positive or negative, and whether you should disengage from the conversation and leave.

| Buying signs | Leaving signs |
| --- | --- |
| Uses your name | No smile or eye contact, no facial expressions |
| Nodding their head with you | Straight face with no reaction to any message |
| Finishes your sentences for you | Stops and blocks us from talking |
| Answers your question | Not answering our questions, or giving short answers |
| Just listens and asks questions | Uses kids, dogs etc. as an excuse |
| Puts the kid or dog away to give you a chance to talk | Rolling their eyes |
| Agrees with you | Crossed arms |
| Listens, pays attention to what you say | Hand on the door handle, door half-way open |
| Biting nails, touching their face, scratching their head (it's a thinking process for some) | Looks not interested, tapping their feet |

**What a buying customer says:** “I've been thinking about it...” · “I've seen the leaflet...” · “I knew about it but didn't know what to do...” · “My mum / friend / auntie uses it...” · “What do I need to do? What happens next?”

**What a leaving customer says:** not much · “Yeah, yeah, yeah, sounds great, but NO” · gives an objection straight away or blocks you · keeps giving objections to every solution

> BEST PRACTICE: Apologise and remove yourself from the situation to safeguard your energy.

## 3 simple steps

### 1 · Agree and empathise

When faced with any objection about the product, our first step is to make sure we don't turn this into a debate. No matter how illogical or silly the reason, we must always start by agreeing and empathising with our customers. Agree by simply using an energetic “Perfect!” Empathise by sharing your own or others' experiences (“I am the same”, or “you sound just like my friend”).

> Customer: “It sounds great, but we just like to get our own milk / do our own shopping.”  
> BA: “Perfect! I am so happy that you said that. I'm actually the same, it's just me and my partner at home and we love to do our shopping together as well!”

> Customer: “This all sounds great, but I'd like to speak to my partner first if that's okay.”  
> BA: “Perfect! Of course! I am so happy that you said that. I am actually the same, I always want to run things by my partner before buying something new for the household.”

### 2 · Investigate

Investigating is simply asking questions to learn more about their objection prior to offering a solution.

- “Where do you typically go food shopping?”
- “How often do you run out of milk?”
- “How many pints of milk do you go through in the week?”
- “Do you find you're pretty busy during the weekdays?”

If the customer is still on the fence, use some positive leading questions (we want them to answer yes!) or try to track down any underlying objections.

- “Do you think this is something you'll use in the future?”
- “What excites you most about using The Modern Milkman?”
- “What are you most hesitant about with The Modern Milkman?”
- “Is there any specific reason why it doesn't interest you today?”

### 3 · Solve

We should finish off handling the objection by offering a solution as to how Modern Milkman will or can work for the customer. Reassure the customer that everything is going to be ok.

- **Relate it to their shopping:** that's what it is, after all!
- **Inform them** of the cut-off, the flexibility, pausing on weeks when needed, the self-managed app.
- **Hold their hand** (not literally): you are the expert. If there was ever a time to do it, now is that time!
- **Make it specific:** put a date to the delivery that will suit the customer.
- **Use:** “Bit of a silly question...”
key_facts: Objections are often signs of interest: the customer is looking for more information
The cycle: Smile & Agree · Relate to others · Feel, Felt, Found · Re-impulse · Close
Pre-empting deals with the negative before it arises; turning deals with it after
Don't undo your efforts by using the word 'BUT'
Three steps: Agree and empathise · Investigate · Solve
Leaving signs: apologise and remove yourself from the situation to safeguard your energy

title: Common Objections
summary: Real-life objections and how to deal with them in a calm and effective way.
body:
## Real-life examples

### 1 · “I still need to go shopping”

- At Modern Milkman we are much more than a “milk delivery”.
- We offer products to complete your breakfast like cereals, bread, butter, croissants, and juices or milkshakes, also a large selection of extras and one-off products.
- We are constantly working on expanding our products in order to cater to all our customers' needs.

### 2 · “Modern Milkman is too expensive”

- Amazing discounts on offer for the first 2 weeks
- Answering “How much does it cost?”: give the price per pint, then ask “How many pints of milk do you use?”

> TIP: Don't shy away. Price and value is a key selling point for us! It's not about the price, it's what the customer gets for it. Create the value in the product and price won't matter.

### 3 · “It's not flexible enough for me”

- Flexible, self-managed weekly repeat orders
- You're in control of your delivery days and orders
- Use it on your terms
- Use it when you need it

> TIP: Questions that evoke an emotional or visual response will typically get the customer talking more. We can create this by acting surprised by their objection, or by trying to drum up a memory about their connection to our products (friends, family, television).

### 4 · The simple “Not interested”

Questions we can ask can vary, but should always try to flush out the real objection that is hidden below their not-interested veil.

- “So, have you used our services before then? Have you heard of us before?”
- “Did you have a bad experience with us before?”
- “Do you have some friends or family who use our services?”

### 5 · The “Not for me”

The main thing to keep in mind is that it's your role to concept the customer that Modern Milkman will benefit their lives.

Examples: I like to do my own shopping · It sounds too expensive · I have fussy kids · I have time to do the shopping myself · I don't drink much milk · I work away · We have too many people in the house (shared house, large family)

### 6 · The “Not right now”

These customers may believe that the product will be suitable but are not certain they should sign today. When you start hearing these objections, don't despair!

Examples: I need to speak to my partner · Can you leave me with a brochure? · I would prefer to do it online in my own time · I just don't have time right now · I might use this in the future but not today · Can you leave me with your code?

## Common objections in the field

### “I don't really drink much milk” (in the introduction)

- Be relaxed
- Say: “Yeah, not many people do nowadays, so how many pints do you think you get through in a normal week?”
- You need to establish if it's a “block”, or if they don't qualify
- If they say 2 or more: “Wow, that's actually more than I was expecting, this would definitely work for you”
- Then establish other items for their regular weekly order: “I assume, like most people around here, you also have juice with breakfast and eat bread, yeah?”

### “I just get my milk from the supermarket”

> “I understand, it's easy enough to get it when you're doing your weekly shop. I'm sure, like most of us, you've still run out of milk a couple of times in the past and had to pop to the shop?”

> “Our customers never have that issue. Also, because you're not overfilling your fridge, as we deliver 3 times a week, it means your fridge works better too.”

### “The supermarket is cheaper though”

> “Definitely, the supermarket is a bit cheaper, but the dairy gets a better price from us for their milk, therefore we are helping the community and our economy.”

> “By using us, you'll be helping to support independent businesses, and you will never run out of milk again, which isn't bad for a couple of pence, is it?”

### “I don't drink milk”

We need to establish if this is just a block. Remember, some people we speak to won't drink milk, but if there are other people in the house, especially children, then the household still buys milk.

> “Oh, cool. How long have you been off dairy? Was it a health thing, or a lifestyle choice?”

> “I assume there are at least a couple of other people in the house. Where do you tend to buy their milk from? Is it the supermarket, like most people?”

### “I'm not sure. Can I just try a couple of pints to see how it goes?” (at the close)

> “Of course you can. The big thing our customers love is that you are in control and it's convenient.”

> “If you usually drink about 8 pints, but you only order 2 from us, you're going to run out of milk, and it's going to be annoying.”

> “What some customers that are a bit unsure are doing is taking their full order from us, and just committing to 4 weeks. This way you actually get to see how convenient and good the service is.”

> “Remember, there's no contract with it. All we're asking you to do is get some milk dropped off at your front door. That's all. 4 weeks is plenty of time for you to fall in love with us, and don't worry, I'll show you how to manage your orders in a minute.”

### The front door is on the pavement, and they are worried about it being stolen

- Firstly, this means that they either had a milkie in the past, or thought about it, which is very positive.
- Let them know that was an issue, which is why, by using us, you get to leave instructions for the driver (“round the back”), and also get to take a photo of exactly where they want the milk delivered.
- Also, our milk will be here by 7:30am, so other customers that use us in the street don't have issues.

### “I used to have a milkie before, but it didn't work for me”

If it's the first time you hear it in the day or territory, you initially have to gather information to use. What was the issue? Maybe monthly payments, late delivery, couldn't change orders.

> “A few people have said that to me today. Which milkie did you use before? What did you find was the issue?”

Then promote why to use us instead.

### “I already have a milkie”

> “Brilliant, and which one do you use?”

By asking this way, you find out for definite if it is a local one, which means they don't qualify, or one of our other competitors. If it is a local supplier, we can offer to deliver things like a veg box, that their local milkie might not do.

### “You've been before”

> “Oh great, so you use us already too, like most of the street?”

> “No? Oh, I guess you were busy last time, probably working or on holiday. That's why we've missed you out.”

"Not interested": ask questions to flush out the real objection
"I already have a milkie": find out which one. A local milkman's customer does not qualify

title: The Close
summary: How to get an agreement, close effectively and time it right.
body:
## Getting an agreement

To close a sale, it is important to ensure that you get an agreement from the customer and that they know they will be signing up for Modern Milkman.

If the customer indicates that they do not want to sign, do not hesitate to ask why: “I understand your decision, but can I ask you what your doubts are about Modern Milkman?” In this way, you relaunch the conversation with the customer. Even if you end up not closing the sale, always end the conversation in a positive way. The customer could always decide to subscribe later.

> HOWEVER, IN NO CIRCUMSTANCES IS IT OK TO BE PUSHY WITH THE SALE. ALWAYS RESPECT THE POTENTIAL CUSTOMERS and CONSOLIDATE THE TERRITORY! Our milkies are delivering in the area, and we want the community to remember us well.

If the customer has indicated that THEY would like to sign up to Modern Milkman, tell them about the discount on offer, explain the weekly repeat orders and proceed with the sale.

### The effective close

- Get the agreement
- Explain how to get involved
- Take control (PET: Point, Explain, Tell; use the pitch card)
- Assume the sale and expect YES: it's a great product
- Be confident and to the point
- Use pre-close and hooklines

> “Bit of a silly question, but if you could get fresh milk (produce) straight from the farm delivered to your doorstep, I assume, like most of the neighbours I've spoken to today, you would jump on our milk round as well, yeah!”

### The first delivery date

We can only offer customers dates within 8 days, to ensure we fill up our rounds and keep our deliveries as efficient as possible. We should always start from the 1st available delivery. A first delivery more than 8 days away is a fail.

### After the sale

After the sale has been completed, REMEMBER to collect the basic details to log your sale:

- Receipt number
- Postcode
- Order value
- Date of sale

## Mastering the close

In sales, CLOSING is generally defined as the moment when a customer decides to get involved. Very few customers will close themselves, even if they really want it: their ego won't allow it. Therefore, it's necessary for us to instigate the close.

If we have done a good job in the early stages of our sales process, we will only need to give a simple nudge to the customer to start the close. It might be as simple as saying, “Grab your phone and I will set you up.”

### When to use a pre-close hookline

Sometimes customers might not be ready to buy at the end of your sales conversation. We can generally tell how ready the customer is by watching for:

- Buying or leaving signs
- Closed off, tense or resistant body language
- Gentle excuses or fob offs: “Sounds great, but maybe next time”, “Sounds great, but I need to think about it”, “Great, but I've got everything”

In that case, it's often a good idea to use a PRE-CLOSE hookline before you commit to a final close. A pre-close is a way to test how ready the customer is to buy. A customer who is not ready will often react to a pre-close by bringing up an objection. Remember that objections are actually a good sign, because if the customer is completely uninterested, they'd just say “no thanks” and show you the door.

### Why close

- Customers will not close themselves
- If we don't instigate the close, they will close us
- Saves time with time wasters
- Draws out the objections

### When and how

- ABC: Always Be Closing
- After using a hookline
- Only close when the customer agrees with you (make them agree twice and then close)
- Be confident: assume in your mind and language that the customer will say yes
- Give the customer an option that ISN'T yes or no
- Use positive but firm body language
- Make it easy, simple and short: “Go grab your phone and I will show you how it works. It only takes 2 minutes, and I will be out of your way.”
- Give people options: “Do you use iPhone or Android?”, “Do you want me to drop you some milk tomorrow or Friday? Which day would be better for you?”
- Break eye contact after closing
- Hand them the pitch card, asking: “Which products do you use the most in a week?”
- Close more than once with positive customers
- Maintain eye contact when nodding and agreeing with the customer

## Timing the close

There is no singular moment when you go in for the close, because closing is something that should happen throughout the sales process. The customer grabbing a phone to sign up on is more of a natural conclusion, not an event.

There are two cardinal sins in connection with timing. The first is trying to close too soon, before the customer has enough information on which to base a decision. The other is to go on for too long and talk yourself out of the sale.

At every stage of the sales conversation, we should be asking questions to ensure that the customer has both understood what has been said and agrees with what has been said. Checking for these “yes responses” will ensure that any doubts, disagreements and objections are brought out and discussed at the appropriate time, and not left to fester.

| Too early | Right time | Too late |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No strong impulse | Impulse is at its highest | Impulse died down |
| Not enough reasons to buy | Excitement point | Too long and boring |
| Objection point | Perfect opportunity to close | Excuse point |
| Puts the customer off | High chances for the customer to get involved | Lost interest |
| Customer is not ready to make a decision (uncomfortable, pushy) |  | Talking too much is a “deal killer” |

### What to do

- Close the customer when they agree with you
- Recognise the customer's buying signs, then close
- Get the customer to agree after you have turned the objections, then close
- Remember the timing of the close comes with experience, so close EVERY CUSTOMER and you will gain the experience needed

### Always use assumptive language

- “I'm guessing, like most people...”
- “I'm assuming, like everyone else...”
- “You have probably noticed...”

> The 3 C's rule: **CLEAR**: talk slowly and clearly. **CONFIDENT**: body language, tone of voice, eye contact. **CONCISE**: keep it simple and to the point.
key_facts: Customers will not close themselves: if we don't instigate the close, they will close us
Only close when the customer agrees with you: make them agree twice, then close
Give options that aren't yes or no: "Do you use iPhone or Android?"
Start from the first available delivery: a first delivery more than 8 days away is a fail
The 3 C's: Clear, Confident, Concise
In no circumstances is it ok to be pushy with the sale

title: Types of Customers
summary: How to understand the customer in front of you and adapt your approach.
body:
## Adapting to the customer

In our introduction, it's important we figure out what type of customer we have in front of us, so we can adapt our approach. “Mirror match” the customer: when the customer is confident, speak with confidence; when the customer is speaking quieter, adapt your voice too.

### Direct

- Straight to the point
- Confident, abrupt, short
- Business-smart people
- Logical: if something makes sense they will do it

**How to approach them:** do not overload them · get to the point (K.I.S.S.) · be confident and honest · firm body language and tone of voice · selective terminology · qualify

### Sensitive

- A bit hesitant at first
- Give the impression they want it but have reservations
- Have smartphones but are not using them as often

**How to approach them:** step-by-step explanation · take your time, relax, explain · slow down with your pitch · be patient with them · guide them through the sign-up process and show them how to use the app

### Ingenious

- Don't overly care what it is
- Bubbly, laugh
- Buy anything because they like you
- Make you feel comfortable

**How to approach them:** build a relationship, relate · pay compliments · be relaxed and show indifference · make them feel special and wanted · pay attention to what they say · treat them like a friend · be yourself, have fun, giggle, laugh

### Conscious

- Want to know facts
- They will test us and our product knowledge with random questions (“Where is your milk / bread from?”)

**How to approach them:** know your product very well, study it · give quick, honest answers · don't guess or make things up: be honest if you don't know the answer · stay calm and composed

## A, B and C customers

| ‘A’ customer | ‘B’ customer | ‘C’ customer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drinks 4–10 pints of milk | Only uses a few pints of milk | Uses very little in comparison to ‘A’ and ‘B’ customers |
| Drinks 1–2 pints of juice | Not many eggs or juice | Not bothered or concerned about the environment or supporting British farms |
| Eats 1–2 dozen eggs | Usually doesn't have much time for us | Hard to find hot spots to impulse them |
| Positive and friendly | Not a main decision maker | Not excited about anything Modern Milkman is offering |
| Has time to talk, complete an order and rehash | More time effective to arrange an appointment for later | Leave these people as quickly and politely as possible |
| Decision maker | Uses technology, but not as much |  |
| Doesn't already use a local supplier | Supporting British farms is not their main concern |  |
| Tech-savvy | Not bothered about the environment as much |  |
| Likes the idea of supporting British farms |  |  |
| Wants to help the environment |  |  |

## Find a “1-minute friend”

- A. Someone who likes you
- B. Someone who likes the product
- C. Someone who likes trying new things

> ABC = ALWAYS BE CONNECTING

Our “1-minute friend” could be: young professionals · single mums and dads · shift workers · mid-aged couples · people working from home · young families · people who love milk · health-conscious people · people who support farms · people conscious about the environment · students · busy families

Four types: Direct, Sensitive, Ingenious, Conscious

Leave 'C' customers as quickly and politely as possible

title: Types of Territories
summary: Understanding demographics to aid our sales success.
body:
## Why?

- Enables you to perform in any territory
- Gives you confidence in what impulses to use
- Allows you to adapt to different customers
- Makes coaching easier
- Develops logical thinking for the future
- Allows us to understand the differences in customers' behaviours
- Removes frustrations from our day
- Keeps us cool, calm, collected
- Helps us deal with challenges more easily
- Develops our emotional intelligence

### Low income

Terraced · apartments · small or no gardens · a mixture of council estates · city

**Impulses:** greed · indifference · fear of loss · Jones · take control

**Tips:** People trust decisions based on feelings. If they like you and it's a good deal saving them money, they will buy. Hustle. BIG INTRO. Be different from the last person. Adapt quickly. Sell yourself. Pre-empt objections. Mainly busy young professionals or working families. Make them like you. Relate to people. There are loads of non-qualifiers, so speak to loads of people. Don't waste time: qualify early.

**KPIs:** 120–140 doors · 5 laps · fewer qualifiers · easy to go around · results mainly based on work ethic

### Middle income

Terraced new builds · semi-detached family homes · nice clean gardens · similar interiors, ring doorbells, playgrounds · estates, working families

**Impulses:** greed · indifference · Jones

**Tips:** People trust logic here. They need to like you and trust you. They buy both feelings and logic. They live on a routine, so they are easy to predict. There are early sales here. They might be straightforward when they open the door. Qualify early. Turn partner objections. Set loads of call backs. Mainly a steady or late day.

**KPIs:** 100–120 doors · 3 laps · loads of qualifiers mixed with non-qualifiers · easy catch up · results mainly based on skillset

### High income

Villages · villas · big driveways and gardens · main streets · business people

**Impulses:** USP · indifference · sense of urgency · logic

**Tips:** People trust logic here. They buy the USPs of the product based on the logic of it. They buy the service, concept and idea. They don't like wasting their time, so get to the point. Keep it short. They may challenge you with questions. Slow down. Be friendly and relaxed. If it's a village, use the village name and people in the village, as they know each other. Talk slower. Work smart.

**KPIs:** 70–100 doors · 3 laps · loads of qualifiers · work smart, a late day · results mainly based on mentality
